subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: What is the primary policy objective behind the clubbing provisions contained in Chapter V (sections 96 to 100) of the Income-tax Act, 2025?

options.A: To discourage taxpayers in higher income brackets from diverting a portion of their income or income-generating assets to family members (such as a spouse or minor child) taxed at lower rates, purely to minimise the transferor's own overall tax burden under the progressive slab system
options.B: To provide an additional tax exemption to taxpayers who transfer assets to family members, thereby encouraging intra-family wealth redistribution
options.C: To simplify the computation of total income by consolidating all family members' incomes into a single combined return, regardless of any tax-avoidance motive
options.D: To penalise taxpayers who receive gifts from relatives by taxing such gifts at a flat, non-progressive rate irrespective of the recipient's own income level

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) To discourage taxpayers in higher income brackets from diverting a portion of their income or income-generating assets to family members (such as a spouse or minor child) taxed at lower rates, purely to minimise the transferor's own overall tax burden under the progressive slab system

Since income-tax on individuals is levied progressively, taxpayers in higher brackets may be tempted to divert income to a spouse, minor child, etc., to reduce their own tax liability. Clubbing provisions counter this by including such diverted income back in the transferor's total income, subject to the specific conditions in sections 96 to 100.

question_html: As per section 98, a transfer is deemed to be 'revocable' if it contains a provision for:

question_html: Mr. Rajesh transfers his house property to a trust for the benefit of Mr. Ramesh until Mr. Ramesh's death (i.e., the transfer is irrevocable during Mr. Ramesh's lifetime, and Mr. Rajesh derives no benefit from the trust income). What is the tax treatment of the house property income, both during Mr. Ramesh's lifetime and after his death?

options.A: The income is taxable in Mr. Rajesh's hands throughout, both before and after Mr. Ramesh's death, since a transfer to a trust is always treated as revocable regardless of any exception under section 97(2)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) During Mr. Ramesh's lifetime, the income from the house property is taxable in the hands of the transferee (the trust), since the section 97(2) exception applies; however, after Mr. Ramesh's death, the transfer becomes revocable (as the underlying purpose of the trust has ended), and the income is thereafter included in the total income of Mr. Rajesh

question_html: Where the asset transferred to a spouse (or son's wife) without adequate consideration is invested by the transferee as capital contribution in a business or as a partner's capital in a firm, section 99(2) prescribes which formula for determining the amount to be included in the transferor's total income?

question_html: An individual transfers a commercial property worth Rs. 40 lakh to his son's wife, receiving in exchange an old, dilapidated asset from her worth only Rs. 2 lakh. Is this transfer 'for adequate consideration' so as to escape clubbing under section 99(1)(b)?

options.A: Yes; any consideration passing between the parties, regardless of its value relative to the asset transferred, is treated as 'adequate consideration' for the purposes of section 99(1)(b)
options.B: The adequacy of consideration is irrelevant where the transferee is a son's wife, since section 99(1)(b) applies regardless of consideration in every case involving a daughter-in-law
options.C: Adequacy is determined solely by whether a written exchange agreement was executed and duly registered, irrespective of the actual values of the assets exchanged
options.D: No; since the value of the consideration received (Rs. 2 lakh) is grossly disproportionate to and far below the value of the asset transferred (Rs. 40 lakh), the transfer is not for adequate consideration, and clubbing under section 99(1)(b) applies to the income from the property

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No; since the value of the consideration received (Rs. 2 lakh) is grossly disproportionate to and far below the value of the asset transferred (Rs. 40 lakh), the transfer is not for adequate consideration, and clubbing under section 99(1)(b) applies to the income from the property

'Adequate consideration' requires that the value given in exchange be reasonably commensurate with the value of the asset transferred. A grossly inadequate exchange (Rs. 2 lakh for an asset worth Rs. 40 lakh) does not satisfy this requirement, so the transfer remains within the scope of section 99(1)(b) clubbing.

question_html: A father gifts a house property to his minor son (not a married daughter) without adequate consideration. What is the correct tax treatment of the resulting rental income?

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: What is meant by a 'cross transfer' in the context of the clubbing provisions, as recognised in CIT v. Keshavji Morarji [1967] 66 ITR 142?

options.A: A single transfer made by one spouse to the other spouse, followed by a subsequent unrelated and independent transfer made in the reverse direction, with no connection between the two transactions
options.B: A transfer of an asset from an individual directly to that individual's own spouse, without any involvement of a third party or any second corresponding transfer
options.C: An arrangement of two (or more) inter-connected and mutual transfers, structured such that each transfer constitutes the consideration for the other, so that the substance of the arrangement is that each transferor has indirectly benefited his own spouse or minor child, even though the direct transfer went to someone else's spouse or child
options.D: A transfer of an asset made by an individual to a registered charitable trust, subsequently followed by a distribution from that trust back to the individual's own family members

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) An arrangement of two (or more) inter-connected and mutual transfers, structured such that each transfer constitutes the consideration for the other, so that the substance of the arrangement is that each transferor has indirectly benefited his own spouse or minor child, even though the direct transfer went to someone else's spouse or child

A cross transfer refers to two or more inter-connected transfers, each constituting the consideration for the other, such that in substance each transferor has indirectly transferred a benefit to his own spouse or minor child (even though the formal, direct gift was made to someone else's spouse or child) - as recognised in CIT v. Keshavji Morarji.

question_html: Where a cross-transfer arrangement is established, how is the resulting income taxed for clubbing purposes?

options.A: The income arising from each transfer is assessed in the hands of the actual direct transferee alone, since a cross-transfer arrangement is treated as two entirely separate and unconnected transactions for tax purposes
options.B: The income from both transfers is assessed jointly in the hands of whichever transferor has the higher total income, regardless of which spouse or child actually benefited from which transfer
options.C: Cross transfers are entirely disregarded for income-tax purposes and no clubbing whatsoever applies to either transfer, since neither transfer is directly between spouses
options.D: The income is assessed as if each transferor had directly transferred the asset/amount to his own spouse (or minor child), and clubbed accordingly in that transferor's own hands under the ordinary clubbing provisions - notwithstanding that the direct gift was actually made to someone else's spouse or child

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The income is assessed as if each transferor had directly transferred the asset/amount to his own spouse (or minor child), and clubbed accordingly in that transferor's own hands under the ordinary clubbing provisions - notwithstanding that the direct gift was actually made to someone else's spouse or child

In a cross-transfer arrangement, the courts look at the substance rather than the form: each transferor is treated as having indirectly transferred the benefit to his OWN spouse or minor child, and the resulting income is clubbed in that transferor's own hands, exactly as if the transfer had been made directly rather than through the reciprocal arrangement.

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: Two brothers cross-transfer gifts of UNEQUAL amounts to each other's spouses (Rs. 6 lakh going one way, Rs. 5 lakh going the other way). To what extent is the income arising from the larger (Rs. 6 lakh) gift clubbed in the first brother's hands?

options.A: Clubbing operates only to the extent of the reciprocal (mutual) amount actually cross-transferred, i.e., to the extent of Rs. 5 lakh (the smaller, matching amount) - not the full Rs. 6 lakh, since only Rs. 5 lakh of the larger gift can be regarded as consideration for, and reciprocal to, the smaller gift
options.B: The full income arising from the entire Rs. 6 lakh gift is clubbed in the first brother's hands, since the existence of any cross-transfer arrangement (regardless of the amounts involved) triggers clubbing of the ENTIRE larger amount
options.C: No clubbing applies at all in this scenario, since the doctrine of cross transfers is confined strictly to transfers of exactly equal amounts made by both parties
options.D: The excess Rs. 1 lakh (the difference between the two amounts) is treated as a separate, ordinary taxable gift in the hands of the recipient spouse, entirely unconnected to any clubbing provision

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Clubbing operates only to the extent of the reciprocal (mutual) amount actually cross-transferred, i.e., to the extent of Rs. 5 lakh (the smaller, matching amount) - not the full Rs. 6 lakh, since only Rs. 5 lakh of the larger gift can be regarded as consideration for, and reciprocal to, the smaller gift

Where cross-transferred amounts are unequal, the reciprocal/mutual character of the arrangement - and hence the clubbing - extends only to the extent of the matching, smaller amount. The excess portion of the larger gift, not matched by any reciprocal transfer, falls outside the cross-transfer doctrine's clubbing consequence.

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: Section 99(3) applies where an individual, who is a member of a Hindu Undivided Family, converts his self-acquired property into HUF property. Which of the following is NOT one of the modes of such conversion contemplated by the provision?

options.A: By impressing such separate property with the character of property belonging to the HUF
options.B: By executing a registered sale deed transferring the property to the HUF for a stated market-value consideration paid in full by the HUF
options.C: By throwing such separate property into the common stock of the HUF
options.D: By transferring such separate property, directly or indirectly, to the HUF otherwise than for adequate consideration

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) By executing a registered sale deed transferring the property to the HUF for a stated market-value consideration paid in full by the HUF

Section 99(3) contemplates conversion by impressing the property with the character of HUF property, throwing it into the common stock, or transferring it (directly or indirectly) to the HUF otherwise than for adequate consideration - a sale for full and adequate market-value consideration is not the kind of conversion this anti-avoidance provision targets.

question_html: Where an individual converts self-acquired property into HUF property under section 99(3), and no partition has yet taken place, in whose total income is the income from that property included?

options.A: The HUF's total income, since legal ownership of the converted property now vests in the HUF as a distinct taxable entity
options.B: The total income of the eldest coparcener of the HUF (the Karta), regardless of whether the Karta is the same person as the individual who converted the property
options.C: The individual's own total income (i.e., the converting member's), notwithstanding that legal ownership has passed to the HUF
options.D: Equally divided among all coparceners of the HUF in proportion to their respective shares, as if a partition had already taken place

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The individual's own total income (i.e., the converting member's), notwithstanding that legal ownership has passed to the HUF

Section 99(3) is an anti-avoidance provision: despite the property having become HUF property as a matter of general law, the income from it CONTINUES to be included in the total income of the INDIVIDUAL who effected the conversion, for so long as no partition has taken place.

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: After a converted HUF property (originally converted under section 99(3)) is partitioned, and a share of the property/income is allotted to the CONVERTING INDIVIDUAL'S SPOUSE, how is that spouse's share of income treated?

options.A: It is assessed entirely as the spouse's own independent income, being wholly outside the scope of any clubbing provision once a valid partition has taken place
options.B: It is assessed in the hands of the HUF as a distinct taxable entity, notwithstanding that a partition has already taken place
options.C: It is exempt from tax altogether, since income arising from a share allotted on partition of an HUF is entirely outside the scope of the Income-tax Act
options.D: It is deemed to have arisen to the spouse from assets indirectly transferred by the individual, so that section 99(1)(a) applies and it is clubbed with the individual's own total income

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It is deemed to have arisen to the spouse from assets indirectly transferred by the individual, so that section 99(1)(a) applies and it is clubbed with the individual's own total income

On partition, the share of income/property allotted to the spouse of the individual who originally converted the property is treated as arising to the spouse by way of an INDIRECT transfer from the individual, so that ordinary spousal clubbing under section 99(1)(a) applies to that share.

subject: Income-tax Law
question_html: Once income from converted property (or a partitioned share of it) has been included in the individual's total income under section 99(3) (or, post-partition, under section 99(1)(a)), what is the consequence for the HUF's or spouse's own separately-computed total income?

options.A: That income is EXCLUDED from the HUF's total income (pre-partition) or from the spouse's own separately-assessed total income (post-partition), so as to avoid double taxation of the same income in two different hands
options.B: No such exclusion applies; the same income continues to be separately assessed in full in both the individual's hands AND the HUF's or spouse's own hands, resulting in the income effectively being taxed twice
options.C: The exclusion applies only if the individual specifically applies in writing to the Assessing Officer for such exclusion within the relevant tax year, this being a mandatory procedural precondition
options.D: The exclusion applies only to 50% of the relevant income, with the remaining 50% continuing to be separately assessed in the HUF's or spouse's own hands as well

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) That income is EXCLUDED from the HUF's total income (pre-partition) or from the spouse's own separately-assessed total income (post-partition), so as to avoid double taxation of the same income in two different hands

To prevent double taxation of the same income, once it stands included in the individual's total income under section 99(3) (pre-partition) or section 99(1)(a) (post-partition, in respect of the spouse's share), that same amount is excluded from the HUF's own total income, or from the spouse's own separately-computed total income, as the case may be.

question_html: Where converted HUF property is partitioned and a share is allotted to the individual's MINOR child, how is the income from that minor child's share treated for clubbing purposes?

question_html: Section 99(5)(d) clarifies that, for the purposes of the clubbing provisions, the expression 'income' includes what?

options.A: Only 'capital gains', to the exclusion of income assessable under any other head of income, such as business income or income from other sources
options.B: Only income that has actually been received in cash by the transferee, to the exclusion of any income accrued but not yet actually received
options.C: 'Loss' - so that the clubbing provisions apply equally where the relevant business, activity, or asset (whose income would otherwise be clubbed) instead produces a loss

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) 'Loss' - so that the clubbing provisions apply equally where the relevant business, activity, or asset (whose income would otherwise be clubbed) instead produces a loss

Section 99(5)(d) provides that 'income' for clubbing purposes includes 'loss' as well - ensuring that where the transferred asset, when deployed by the transferee, results in a LOSS rather than a profit, that loss is equally clubbed (i.e., attributed) to the transferor, consistent with how a profit would have been clubbed.

question_html: Mrs. T invests a gifted amount received from her husband as capital in a proprietary business, which results in a business LOSS for the relevant tax year (rather than a profit). What is the effect of section 99(5)(d) on this loss?

options.A: The loss is simply disregarded for clubbing purposes altogether, since section 99(5)(d) applies only to positive income and has no application whatsoever to a loss situation
options.B: The loss is clubbed with the husband's income, but only to the extent of 50% of the loss actually incurred, this being a specific statutory limitation under section 99(5)(d)
options.C: The loss must instead be carried forward indefinitely in Mrs. T's own hands, being entirely outside the scope of any clubbing provision
options.D: The loss (computed by reference to the same proportionate principles that would apply to a profit) is clubbed with - i.e., attributed to - the husband's total income, exactly as a corresponding profit would have been clubbed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The loss (computed by reference to the same proportionate principles that would apply to a profit) is clubbed with - i.e., attributed to - the husband's total income, exactly as a corresponding profit would have been clubbed

By deeming 'income' to include 'loss', section 99(5)(d) ensures symmetrical treatment: just as a profit from the transferee's use of a transferred/gifted asset would be clubbed with the transferor, a resulting LOSS is equally clubbed with (attributed to) the transferor's total income.

On 1.4.2026, Mr. Devansh gifts her a further Rs. 6,00,000, which she invests as additional capital in the same business on the very same day. For the tax year 2026-27, the business earns a profit of Rs. 3,20,000.
question_html: What is the value of 'D' (the transferee's total capital investment in the business) for the purposes of the section 99(2) formula?

options.A: Rs. 6,00,000 (only the gifted capital, with Mrs. Devansh's own pre-existing capital being excluded from 'D')
options.B: Rs. 8,00,000 (Mrs. Devansh's own pre-existing capital of Rs. 2,00,000 plus the gifted capital of Rs. 6,00,000)
options.C: Rs. 2,00,000 (only Mrs. Devansh's own pre-existing capital, with the gifted amount being excluded from 'D')
options.D: Rs. 3,20,000 (the business profit for the year, which is not relevant to the determination of 'D' at all)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Rs. 8,00,000 (Mrs. Devansh's own pre-existing capital of Rs. 2,00,000 plus the gifted capital of Rs. 6,00,000)

'D' represents the transferee's TOTAL capital investment in the business, from all sources. Here, that is Mrs. Devansh's own pre-existing Rs. 2,00,000 plus the gifted Rs. 6,00,000, i.e., Rs. 8,00,000.

question_html: Applying the section 99(2) formula A = B x C/D, what amount is includible in Mr. Devansh's total income for the tax year?

options.B: Rs. 80,000 (3,20,000 x 2,00,000/8,00,000, incorrectly using Mrs. Devansh's own capital rather than the gifted capital as 'C')

case_facts_html: Mr. and Mrs. Bhargava have twin 10-year-old minor daughters, each earning Rs. 2,200 p.a. as passive interest on bank deposits gifted by grandparents. Their 15-year-old minor son earns Rs. 60,000 p.a. from acting in television commercials (a skill-based activity), and separately earns Rs. 4,000 p.a. as bank interest on a fixed deposit made out of his own acting income. Mr. Bhargava's total income (before any clubbing) is Rs. 5,00,000, and Mrs. Bhargava's total income (before any clubbing) is Rs. 4,50,000. Both parents exercise the option to shift out of the default tax regime for the relevant tax year.
question_html: Is the minor son's Rs. 60,000 acting income clubbed with either parent's total income?

options.A: No; the acting income is excluded from clubbing under section 99(1)(c), since it arises from the application of the minor son's own skill and talent, and is instead taxed independently in the minor son's own hands
options.B: Yes, it is clubbed in full with Mr. Bhargava's total income, since Mr. Bhargava's income (before clubbing) is the higher of the two parents' incomes
options.C: Yes, it is clubbed in full with Mrs. Bhargava's total income, since a minor's earned income is always clubbed with the mother specifically, regardless of either parent's income level
options.D: Yes, but only 50% of it is clubbed, with the balance being taxed independently in the minor son's own hands as a specific statutory apportionment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No; the acting income is excluded from clubbing under section 99(1)(c), since it arises from the application of the minor son's own skill and talent, and is instead taxed independently in the minor son's own hands

Section 99(1)(c) excludes from clubbing any income arising from an activity involving the application of the minor's own skill, talent, or specialised knowledge and experience. Acting in television commercials is precisely such a skill-based activity, so the Rs. 60,000 is NOT clubbed and is taxed in the minor son's own hands.

question_html: Is the minor son's Rs. 4,000 bank interest (earned on a deposit made out of his acting income) clubbed with a parent's total income?

options.A: No; since the source of the deposited funds (the acting income) is itself excluded from clubbing, any further income earned by investing those funds is equally excluded from clubbing, on the same 'skill income' reasoning
options.B: Yes; although the underlying acting income itself is excluded from clubbing, the bank interest is 'accretion' income arising from investment of that acting income, and ordinary accretion income of a minor child IS clubbed under the general rule in section 99(1)(c) (the skill/talent exception applies only to the skill-based income itself, not to further income earned by investing it)
options.C: No; bank interest earned by a minor child is, in every case and regardless of source, entirely outside the scope of section 99(1)(c) clubbing
options.D: Yes, but only to the extent of 50% of the interest, with the balance being taxed independently in the minor son's own hands

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes; although the underlying acting income itself is excluded from clubbing, the bank interest is 'accretion' income arising from investment of that acting income, and ordinary accretion income of a minor child IS clubbed under the general rule in section 99(1)(c) (the skill/talent exception applies only to the skill-based income itself, not to further income earned by investing it)

The skill/talent exclusion under section 99(1)(c) applies only to income directly arising from the exercise of the minor's own skill or talent - it does not extend to further income earned by investing that skill-based income. The Rs. 4,000 bank interest is ordinary passive income of the minor child and is clubbed under the general rule.

Both parents exercise the option to shift out of the default tax regime for the relevant tax year.
question_html: Applying the Rs. 1,500-per-minor-child Schedule III exemption (available since both parents have opted out of the default regime), what total amount is clubbed with Mr. Bhargava's total income?

options.A: Rs. 5,900 - being the full, un-exempted total of the daughters' Rs. 4,400 interest and the son's Rs. 4,000 accretion-interest, plus the son's Rs. 60,000 acting income, before any Schedule III exemption is applied
options.B: Rs. 8,400 - being the daughters' Rs. 4,400 interest and the son's Rs. 4,000 accretion-interest, both taken in full without any Schedule III exemption being applied at all
options.C: Rs. 3,900 - being the twin daughters' combined interest of Rs. 4,400 less the Rs. 3,000 exemption (Rs. 1,500 x 2 daughters) = Rs. 1,400, PLUS the son's Rs. 4,000 accretion-interest less the Rs. 1,500 exemption = Rs. 2,500, totalling Rs. 1,400 + Rs. 2,500 = Rs. 3,900
options.D: Rs. 64,000 - being the son's full Rs. 60,000 acting income plus his Rs. 4,000 accretion-interest, with the daughters' interest being disregarded entirely

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Rs. 3,900 - being the twin daughters' combined interest of Rs. 4,400 less the Rs. 3,000 exemption (Rs. 1,500 x 2 daughters) = Rs. 1,400, PLUS the son's Rs. 4,000 accretion-interest less the Rs. 1,500 exemption = Rs. 2,500, totalling Rs. 1,400 + Rs. 2,500 = Rs. 3,900

Since Mr. Bhargava's income (Rs. 5,00,000) exceeds Mrs. Bhargava's (Rs. 4,50,000), all clubbable minor-child income is clubbed with him. Daughters: Rs. 2,200 x 2 = Rs. 4,400 - Rs. 1,500 x 2 = Rs. 1,400 taxable. Son's accretion-interest: Rs. 4,000 - Rs. 1,500 = Rs. 2,500 taxable. Total clubbed = Rs. 1,400 + Rs. 2,500 = Rs. 3,900 (the son's Rs. 60,000 acting income is excluded entirely, being skill-income, and is not part of this clubbed total at all).

case_facts_html: On 1.4.2026, Mr. Farhan transfers a house property to Mrs. Farhan without any consideration, and there is no agreement between them to live apart. The computed annual rental income from the house property for the tax year 2026-27 is Rs. 1,80,000.
question_html: Which provision governs the tax treatment of the Rs. 1,80,000 rental income in this scenario?

options.A: Section 99(1)(a)(ii), which clubs income from an asset (other than house property) transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration
options.B: Section 99(1)(c), the minor-child clubbing provision, since Mrs. Farhan is treated as a dependent of Mr. Farhan for this purpose
options.C: Section 96, since the arrangement amounts to a transfer of income without transfer of the underlying asset
options.D: Section 25(a), which deems Mr. Farhan (the transferor) to continue to be the owner of the house property for income-tax purposes, since it was transferred to his spouse without adequate consideration and there is no agreement to live apart

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Section 25(a), which deems Mr. Farhan (the transferor) to continue to be the owner of the house property for income-tax purposes, since it was transferred to his spouse without adequate consideration and there is no agreement to live apart

Section 25(a) specifically governs a house property transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration (absent an agreement to live apart) - it deems the TRANSFEROR to continue to be the owner for tax purposes, displacing the general asset-transfer clubbing rule of section 99(1)(a)(ii), which is expressly confined to assets OTHER THAN house property.

The Schedule III Sl. No. 17 exemption of Rs. 1,500 applies only to clubbed MINOR-CHILD income under section 99(1)(c) - not to spousal-remuneration clubbing under section 99(1)(a)(i). So: Mrs. Chatterjee's salary clubs in full at Rs. 3,00,000, and the minor son's interest clubs at Rs. 18,000 - Rs. 1,500 = Rs. 16,500, for a total of Rs. 3,16,500 clubbed with Mr. Chatterjee's total income.
topic_text: CS10 - Total Amount Clubbed with Mr. Chatterjee's Total Income
exam_applicability: Applicable for the September 2026 and January 2027 CA Inter examinations onwards. This chapter is based on the Income-tax Act, 2025 and reflects the position of law existing as on 30.04.2026, per the ICAI Study Material. Coverage includes the clubbing of income provisions under Chapter V (sections 96 to 100): transfer of income without transfer of asset (section 96), chargeability of income arising from a revocable transfer of assets and the meaning of 'transfer'/'revocable transfer' (sections 97 and 98) including the specific exceptions under section 97(2), clubbing of a spouse's remuneration from a concern in which the individual has a substantial interest and the technical/professional-qualification exception (section 99(1)(a)(i)), clubbing of income from an asset transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration including the interplay with section 25(a) for house property and the proportionate-income formula for assets invested in a business/firm (sections 99(1)(a)(ii) and 99(2)), clubbing of income from an asset transferred to a son's wife (section 99(1)(b)), clubbing of a minor child's income and the specific exclusions for skill/talent/work income and disability under section 154, together with the Schedule III (Table: Sl. No. 17) exemption of up to Rs. 1,500 per minor child (section 99(1)(c)), clubbing of income from assets transferred to any person/ AOP for the benefit of a spouse or son's wife (section 99(1)(d)), the cross-transfer doctrine, conversion of self-acquired property into HUF property and its treatment on partition (section 99(3)), the rule that 'income' includes 'loss' (section 99(5)(d)), and the distinction between sections 96/97 and section 99.
